conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers and birthing parents. Today I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**—a tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply a conversation starter, not a test of any kind, and everything you share stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your safety or your baby’s.

We’ll go through ten questions about the past seven days. You can answer in your own words—there are no right or wrong answers—and if anything feels confusing, just let me know and we’ll sort it out together.

Ready to begin?  
First, how have you been able to enjoy things lately—those little moments of laughter or pleasure that used to feel easy before the baby came?

Honestly? Most things feel… flat. I’ll put the baby down for a nap and think “great, I could watch that show I used to love,” but five minutes in I’m just staring at the screen. Even when my partner tries to make me laugh, it feels like I have to fake it so I don’t hurt his feelings. The only thing that still sparks a little warmth is when the baby smiles at me, but even that’s short-lived because I immediately worry I’m not doing enough to keep her happy.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, every now and then something small will catch me off-guard and I’ll sort of half-laugh, but it’s like the sound surprises me and then it’s gone. Mostly I feel too tired or on-edge to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. When I think about the weekend coming up, or a coffee date a friend keeps trying to plan, I just feel… blank, like “what’s the point?” I used to get excited about little outings or even just a quiet hour to myself, but now it all feels like another chore I have to pretend I want.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often, actually. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I didn’t feed her right or I missed some cue. Last night she wouldn’t settle, and I laid there wondering what I did wrong—maybe I ate something that bothered her through the milk, or I held her too much today. My head tells me babies just cry, but I still feel like I must be failing somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, a lot of the time. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s too quiet—so I run to the bassinet to check she’s breathing. Or I lie awake picturing her tiny body overheating, or the crib sheet somehow covering her face even though it’s fitted tight. I know it sounds irrational, but in the moment it feels so real I can’t shake it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it hits out of nowhere—like yesterday I was warming a bottle and suddenly felt this wave of dread, my chest went tight, and I had to put her down in the crib just so I could sit on the floor and breathe. I couldn’t tell you what I was actually scared of; it just felt like something awful was about to happen.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finally get her down, then notice the sink’s full of bottles, the laundry’s mountain-high, and I still haven’t eaten. I’ll stand in the middle of the mess and feel this pressure in my chest, like I’m drowning in stuff I can’t keep up with. I usually push through, but it’s exhausting and I end up snapping at my partner over nothing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind just spins—replaying every little thing I did that day, worrying I missed something, or imagining all the ways something could go wrong tomorrow. Some nights I drift off, then jolt awake sure I heard her cry. Even when she’s sound asleep, I can’t settle. I end up staring at the ceiling for hours, and by morning I feel even more drained.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s… most of the week, really. I’ll be feeding her and tears just start slipping down my face for no clear reason. Everything feels gray—like I’m stuck under a heavy blanket I can’t kick off. Some moments are better, but the sadness always circles back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times this week. Sometimes it’s when I’m rocking her at 3 a.m. and she won’t settle; I’ll just start crying with her. Other times it’s smaller—like seeing a happy family on social media and suddenly feeling like I’m failing at all of it. The tears come quick, and afterward I feel even more worn-out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never felt like I wanted to be gone or to do anything like that. I just want to feel like myself again and be a good mom.

You've shared that the joy you once felt has faded; even the smallest pleasures now feel distant, and laughter comes only in brief, surprising moments. Days are clouded by a heavy, gray sadness that brings tears without warning, while anxious thoughts race through your mind-especially about your baby's safety-sometimes erupting into sudden waves of panic. Everyday tasks feel overwhelming, as though you're drowning in bottles and laundry, yet you push through, blaming yourself whenever anything seems amiss. Sleep offers little relief because worries replay the moment your head touches the pillow, and you wake already depleted, longing to feel like yourself again and to be the mother you want to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes only rare, fleeting half-laughs and a persistent inability to find things funny, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses near-complete anhedonia, describing feelings as 'blank' and activities as pointless, aligning with 'Hardly at all</sym>, <sym>"Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense, intrusive worries about infant safety that arise without real threat, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, inexplicable panic episodes ('wave of dread', chest tightness, need to sit and breathe) occurring 'sometimes', aligning with 'Yes, sometimes'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to keep up, and emotionally drowning—clearly matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to racing anxious thoughts and hypervigilance, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most of the week" with uncontrollable crying and persistent low mood, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent crying episodes this week, triggered by both exhaustion and emotional comparison, fitting 'quite often</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 23 places patient well above EPDS threshold of ≥14 for probable major depression. She endorses core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, fatigue, diminished ability to think or concentrate, and sleep disturbance, all persisting most days for the past week with clear functional impact. High anxiety item scores and descriptions of abrupt chest-tightening dread also indicate comorbid postpartum anxiety/panic symptoms. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for diagnostic evaluation and treatment planning
2. Call local postpartum support line or warmline for immediate emotional support
3. Discuss with partner or trusted adult to share baby-care duties overnight to allow 4-5 hours consolidated sleep
4. Begin simple self-care: daily 10-minute outdoor walk, balanced meals, hydration; accept help with housework
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
6. If thoughts of self-harm develop, seek emergency care or call emergency services
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-maternal self-report (verbal administration)

Symptoms endorsed (frequency/intensity):  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Marked guilt/self-blame re infant care  
- Generalized anxiety with intrusive "worst-case" cognitions; two recent panic-equivalent episodes (chest tightness, need to sit/lay infant down)  
- Middle & initial insomnia related to rumination and hypervigilance about infant safety  
- Feeling "overwhelmed/drowning" most days; difficulty coping with routine tasks  
- Spontaneous crying spells, "gray" emotional tone throughout week  
- Absence of enjoyment toward previously pleasant activities  

Pattern: Consistent with moderate–severe depressive and anxiety symptoms, postpartum onset (≤ 12 wks).

Areas of screening significance  
- Postpartum depression (high endorsement: items 1,2,6,7,8,9)  
- Postpartum anxiety/panic spectrum (items 4,5)  
- Maternal role-related guilt and functional impairment (item 3,6)  

Risk factors identified  
✓ Sleep disruption secondary to mood rather than solely infant demands  
✓ Excessive maternal self-blame/guilt  
✓ Panic-equivalent episodes while infant in arms (safety consideration)  

Safety screen  
- Denies self-harm thoughts (item 10) – no current suicidal ideation reported  

Overall screening impression: High clinical likelihood of postpartum major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety symptoms; parent functioning significantly impacted. Further diagnostic evaluation and discussion of support options recommended.
